notes.front: What is container orchestration?
notes.back: Managing and automating the lifecycle of containerised applications in changing environments: deploying, scaling, healing and monitoring them.
notes.explanation: You declare how the system should look, and the orchestrator watches it and corrects any deviation, such as starting a new container when one crashes.
notes.example: Like a conductor making sure every musician plays their part; in most cases, the orchestrator is Kubernetes.

notes.front: Does Kubernetes try to be a complete, all-in-one platform?
notes.back: No. It provides building blocks for developer platforms and leaves many choices, such as logging and monitoring tools, to you.
notes.explanation: Its PaaS-like features are optional and pluggable, which preserves user choice and flexibility.
notes.example: You pick your own monitoring tools and plug them in, instead of getting one fixed stack.

notes.front: What is a Kubernetes cluster?
notes.back: A set of worker machines, called nodes, that run containerised applications; every cluster has at least one worker node.
notes.explanation: Everything Kubernetes manages lives in a cluster, and the cluster also contains the components that manage it.
notes.example: Three virtual machines working together to run a company’s web shop under Kubernetes.

notes.front: What is the Kubernetes control plane?
notes.back: The part of Kubernetes that runs the cluster: it takes your requests, decides where things run, and keeps checking they do.
notes.explanation: The glossary calls it “the container orchestration layer that exposes the API and interfaces to define, deploy, and manage the lifecycle of containers”; its components make global decisions, such as scheduling.
notes.example: The part of the cluster that decides what should run where, as opposed to the machines that run it.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is a Node?
notes.back: A worker machine, virtual or physical, that runs the services needed to run containers and is managed by the control plane.
notes.explanation: It is the general idea of a node, made specific: the machines of a Kubernetes cluster where applications actually run.
notes.example: One of three VMs in a cluster, each running a kubelet and a container runtime.

notes.front: What is a Pod, in one sentence?
notes.back: The smallest and simplest Kubernetes unit: a set of one or more running containers on your cluster.
notes.explanation: The containers in a Pod are placed and scheduled together on the same node; a Pod usually runs one main container.
notes.example: A Pod running a single web server container.

notes.front: What is the Kubernetes data plane?
notes.back: The layer that provides capacity, such as CPU, memory, network and storage, so that containers can run and connect to a network.
notes.explanation: The control plane decides; the data plane supplies the resources where the work happens.
notes.example: The CPU, memory and disks of a cluster’s worker nodes.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what does “master” mean?
notes.back: A legacy term for the nodes that host the control plane.
notes.explanation: Current documentation says control plane; some provisioning tools and managed services still use the old word.
notes.example: Older guides saying “the master node” mean the machine running the control plane.

notes.front: What is kube-apiserver?
notes.back: The control plane component that exposes the Kubernetes HTTP API; it is the front end of the control plane.
notes.explanation: Users, the parts of the cluster and external components all communicate with one another through the API server.
notes.example: Any request to create or change something in the cluster goes to the API server first.

notes.front: What is etcd?
notes.back: The database holding all Kubernetes cluster data as named entries (keys) with values; it is built to stay correct and available if a machine fails.
notes.explanation: It holds all the API server’s data, so if your cluster uses etcd you need a plan for backing it up.
notes.example: The record of every Pod, Node and setting in the cluster lives in etcd.

notes.front: What is kube-scheduler?
notes.back: The control plane component that watches for newly created Pods with no node assigned, and selects a node for each to run on.
notes.explanation: It weighs resource requirements, hardware, software and policy constraints, affinity rules, data locality and more.
notes.example: A new Pod needs two CPUs; the scheduler picks a node that has two CPUs free.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is a controller?
notes.back: A control loop that watches the state of the cluster and makes or requests changes to move the current state towards the desired state.
notes.explanation: A thermostat is one: you set the desired temperature, and it turns the heating on or off to reach it.
notes.example: The node controller notices when a node goes down and responds.

notes.front: What is kube-controller-manager?
notes.back: The control plane component that runs the controller processes.
notes.explanation: Each controller is logically separate, but they are packaged as one program and run as one process to keep things simple.
notes.example: The node controller, which notices and responds when nodes go down, runs inside it.

notes.front: What is cloud-controller-manager?
notes.back: An optional control plane component that embeds cloud-specific logic and links your cluster to your cloud provider’s API.
notes.explanation: It separates the parts that talk to the cloud platform from those that only deal with the cluster, so providers can release features at their own pace.
notes.example: When the cluster asks for a load balancer, a controller in it creates one from the cloud provider.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is a Service?
notes.back: A way to expose a network application running as one or more Pods, so traffic reaches whichever Pods currently run it.
notes.explanation: As Pods are added or removed, the Service makes sure traffic is directed to the current set.
notes.example: A “web” Service that sends requests to three identical web server Pods.

notes.front: What is service discovery?
notes.back: The process of finding the individual instances that currently make up a service.
notes.explanation: In cloud native systems apps restart often and get new addresses each time, so clients need a common place to look them up.
notes.example: Like a switchboard that always knows which desk a colleague has moved to today.

notes.front: What is a proxy, in networking?
notes.back: A server that acts as an intermediary: the client talks to the proxy, which passes the request to the real server and relays the reply.
notes.explanation: In Kubernetes, a network proxy on each node implements part of the Service concept.
notes.example: Like a receptionist who takes your question, asks the expert, and brings back the answer.

notes.front: What is kube-proxy?
notes.back: An optional network proxy on each node that maintains the network rules implementing Services.
notes.explanation: Those rules let network sessions from inside or outside the cluster reach your Pods.
notes.example: A request for the “web” Service arrives at a node; rules kept by kube-proxy pass it to one of the web Pods.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what are addons?
notes.back: Resources that extend the functionality of Kubernetes, providing cluster-level features.
notes.explanation: They are optional extras on top of the core components, though every cluster should have cluster DNS.
notes.example: The Dashboard, a web interface for managing a cluster, is an addon.

notes.front: What is the Kubernetes API?
notes.back: The application that serves Kubernetes functionality through a RESTful interface and stores the state of the cluster.
notes.explanation: Every change in the cluster is a call to this API, whether made directly or through command-line tools.
notes.example: Asking the cluster to run a new Pod is an API request to the API server.

notes.front: What is a Kubernetes object?
notes.back: A persistent entity in the Kubernetes system that represents part of the state of your cluster; a “record of intent”.
notes.explanation: Once you create an object, Kubernetes works constantly to make sure what it describes actually exists.
notes.example: A Pod, a Service or a Node is each represented by an object.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Understanding Kubernetes objects”

notes.front: What is an object’s spec?
notes.back: The field in which you describe the characteristics you want the object to have: its desired state.
notes.explanation: You set it when you create the object, and the control plane works to make reality match it.
notes.example: A spec saying three copies of an application should be running.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Object spec and status”

notes.front: What is an object’s status?
notes.back: The field describing the object’s current state, supplied and updated by Kubernetes and its components.
notes.explanation: The control plane compares status with spec and corrects any difference.
notes.example: A status showing that two of the three requested copies are running.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Object spec and status”

notes.front: What is YAML?
notes.back: A human-friendly text format for writing structured data, widely used for configuration files.
notes.explanation: Most lines pair a name with a value, and indentation shows what belongs to what, so people can read and edit it easily.
notes.example: A file containing the line “name: web” is a tiny piece of YAML.
notes.source: YAML Ain’t Markup Language (YAML) version 1.2.2, Abstract and §1
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence for adaptation; facts in our own words

notes.front: What is JSON?
notes.back: JavaScript Object Notation: a lightweight, text-based data format that programs in any language can exchange.
notes.explanation: The Kubernetes API exchanges data as JSON; YAML is the more readable choice for files people write by hand.
notes.example: {"name": "web"} is a tiny piece of JSON.
notes.source: IETF RFC 8259, “The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format”, Abstract; Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”
notes.sourceLicence: C · IETF Trust; facts in our own words

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is a manifest?
notes.back: A specification of a Kubernetes API object in JSON or YAML format.
notes.explanation: It gives the desired state that Kubernetes will maintain when you apply the manifest.
notes.example: A YAML file describing a Pod: its name, its container and the image to use.

notes.front: What is an API group?
notes.back: A set of related paths in the Kubernetes API, named in the REST path and in an object’s apiVersion field.
notes.explanation: apiVersion is the manifest field naming the API version. Groups make the Kubernetes API easier to extend, and each can be enabled or disabled on the API server.
notes.example: The group rbac.authorization.k8s.io, whose version v1alpha1 is served at /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1alpha1.

notes.front: What is a Kubernetes API version?
notes.back: One of several versions at which an API is served, each at its own path, such as /api/v1 or /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1alpha1.
notes.explanation: Versioning at the API level lets Kubernetes restructure or remove fields cleanly; different versions show the same stored data.
notes.example: An object created through v1beta1 can later be read or updated through v1.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “The Kubernetes API”, “API groups and versioning”

notes.front: What are the three stability levels of a Kubernetes API version?
notes.back: Alpha, beta and generally available (GA), from least to most stable.
notes.explanation: The level decides how long a version must be kept: the more stable it is, the stronger the compatibility promise.
notes.example: v1alpha1 is an alpha version and v1beta1 a beta version; GA versions are typically v1.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What is an object’s name in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A client-provided string that refers to an object, unique among objects of the same kind at any one time.
notes.explanation: If you delete the object, you can create a new one with the same name.
notes.example: Only one Pod can be called myapp-1234 at a time, but a Pod and a Service can both use that name.

notes.front: What is an object’s UID in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A system-generated string that uniquely identifies an object across the whole lifetime of the cluster.
notes.explanation: It tells apart historical occurrences of similar objects, even ones with the same name.
notes.example: Delete a Pod and recreate it with the same name: the new Pod gets a different UID.

notes.front: What is a namespace in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A way to isolate groups of resources within a single cluster; names must be unique within a namespace, but not across namespaces.
notes.explanation: Namespaces divide one cluster between many users, teams or projects.
notes.example: A “shop” namespace and a “blog” namespace can each hold a Service called web.

notes.front: What are the initial namespaces of a Kubernetes cluster?
notes.back: The four namespaces every new cluster starts with, including default and kube-system.
notes.explanation: Each has a set purpose, so knowing them tells you where your own objects and the system’s objects live.
notes.example: Listing the namespaces of a brand-new cluster shows default, kube-node-lease, kube-public and kube-system.

notes.front: What is a label in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A key/value pair attached to an object to give it identifying attributes that are meaningful to users.
notes.explanation: Labels are used to organise objects and to select subsets of them.
notes.example: environment: production and tier: frontend on a Pod.

notes.front: What is a label selector?
notes.back: An expression that filters a list of objects by their labels, identifying a set of objects.
notes.explanation: The label selector is the core grouping primitive in Kubernetes.
notes.example: Selecting every Pod labelled tier: frontend.

notes.front: What is an annotation in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A key/value pair used to attach arbitrary, non-identifying metadata to an object.
notes.explanation: Tools and libraries can read annotations, but annotations are not used to identify or select objects.
notes.example: A note recording which build produced an object, or who to contact about it.

notes.front: What is a field selector?
notes.back: A filter that selects Kubernetes objects by the value of one or more of their resource fields.
notes.explanation: All resource types support selecting on metadata.name and metadata.namespace.
notes.example: Selecting the Pod whose metadata.name is web-1.
introduces: field selectors, owners and dependents, finalizers, garbage collection
uses: field selectors, owners and dependents, finalizers, garbage collection

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is an owner reference?
notes.back: A field on a dependent object pointing to the object that owns it.
notes.explanation: Owner references tell the control plane which objects depend on others, so related objects can be cleaned up together.
notes.example: Pods created on behalf of another object carry an owner reference to it.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is garbage collection?
notes.back: The collective term for the mechanisms Kubernetes uses to clean up cluster resources.
notes.explanation: It removes things like terminated Pods, unused containers and images, and objects whose owners are gone.
notes.example: After an owner object is deleted, its dependent objects are cleaned up automatically.

notes.front: What is a finalizer?
notes.back: A label-like key (e.g. kubernetes.io/pv-protection) that makes Kubernetes wait for clean-up before it finally deletes an object.
notes.explanation: Finalizers alert controllers to clean up what the deleted object owned.
notes.example: kubernetes.io/pv-protection stops a PersistentVolume object (a storage object, see Storage) being deleted while a Pod still uses it.

notes.front: In the Kubernetes API, what is a watch?
notes.back: A kind of API request that keeps a connection open and streams every change to an object.
notes.explanation: It detects changes efficiently: a controller can watch instead of polling repeatedly.
notes.example: A controller watches its objects and reacts the moment one changes.

notes.front: In Kubernetes, what is an Event?
notes.back: An object that describes a state change or other notable occurrence in the cluster.
notes.explanation: Events are kept for a limited time and are informative, best-effort data: useful for understanding what happened.
notes.example: An Event recording that the scheduler assigned a Pod to a node.

notes.front: What is a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)?
notes.back: A kind of API object that defines a new custom API to add to your Kubernetes API server, without building a complete custom server.
notes.explanation: It lets you extend the Kubernetes API when the built-in resources cannot meet your needs.
notes.example: Defining a new resource type called SampleDB, which the API server then serves and stores.

notes.front: What is a custom resource?
notes.back: An extension of the Kubernetes API that is not necessarily in a default installation, added through a CRD or API aggregation.
notes.explanation: Once installed, users create and access its objects just as they do built-in ones like Pods.
notes.example: SampleDB objects, available once the SampleDB CRD is installed.

notes.front: What is the operator pattern?
notes.back: A design that links a controller to one or more custom resources, to automate managing an application.
notes.explanation: It captures in code what a human operator knows about running a particular service.
notes.example: An operator that deploys a database, takes and restores its backups and handles its upgrades.

notes.front: What is the Kubernetes aggregation layer?
notes.back: A mechanism that lets you install additional Kubernetes-style APIs, served by your own API server behind the main one.
notes.explanation: The main API server passes requests for those resources to your server, so the API looks extended to users.
notes.example: A team runs its own API server for a resource that needs custom storage, and the main API server forwards requests to it.

notes.front: What is a feature gate?
notes.back: A key that controls whether a particular Kubernetes feature is enabled in your cluster.
notes.explanation: Each component has its own set, turned on or off with its --feature-gates flag.
notes.example: Turning on an alpha feature for testing in a development cluster.

notes.front: What does the name Kubernetes mean?
notes.back: It comes from Greek, meaning helmsman or pilot.
notes.explanation: The project is often shortened to K8s.

notes.front: Why is Kubernetes abbreviated “K8s”?
notes.back: The 8 counts the eight letters between the “K” and the “s”.
notes.explanation: So “K8s” and “Kubernetes” name the same project.

notes.front: Who open-sourced Kubernetes, and when?
notes.back: Google, in 2014.
notes.explanation: It combines over 15 years of Google’s experience running production workloads at scale with ideas from the community.

notes.front: In most cases, what is the container orchestrator used for cloud native applications?
notes.back: Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: The CNCF glossary calls Kubernetes an open source container orchestrator, like a “datacenter operating system”.
notes.source: Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Container Orchestration”; Cloud Native Glossary (CNCF), “Kubernetes”

notes.front: Is Kubernetes a traditional, all-inclusive PaaS?
notes.back: No. It offers some PaaS-like features, such as deployment and scaling, but they are optional and pluggable.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes operates at the container level and provides building blocks for developer platforms, preserving user choice.

notes.front: Does Kubernetes build your application from source code?
notes.back: No. It does not deploy source code or build applications.
notes.explanation: How code gets built and delivered is left to each organisation’s own tools and processes.

notes.front: Does Kubernetes dictate which logging, monitoring or alerting tools you use?
notes.back: No. It provides some integrations as proof of concept, and mechanisms to collect and export metrics.
notes.explanation: You integrate your own logging, monitoring and alerting solutions.

notes.front: Does Kubernetes provide databases, message buses or caches as built-in services?
notes.back: No. Such components can run on Kubernetes, but they are not built in.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes does not provide application-level services such as middleware or data-processing frameworks.

notes.front: Why does the Kubernetes documentation say Kubernetes is not a mere orchestration system?
notes.back: It uses independent control processes that continuously drive the current state towards the desired state, instead of a fixed workflow.
notes.explanation: Orchestration in the strict sense means “first do A, then B, then C”; Kubernetes does not care how you get from A to C.

notes.front: Kubernetes can expose a container using a DNS name or its own IP address, and spread traffic when it is high. Which capability is this?
notes.back: Service discovery and load balancing.
notes.explanation: Spreading the network traffic keeps the application stable under load.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: You scale an application up and down with a simple command, a UI, or automatically based on CPU usage. Which Kubernetes capability is this?
notes.back: Horizontal scaling.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes changes the number of running copies, not the size of each machine.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: You can add features to a Kubernetes cluster without changing upstream source code. Which design property is this?
notes.back: Designed for extensibility.
notes.explanation: Features are added to the cluster, not to Kubernetes’ own code.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Overview”, “Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do”

notes.front: How many worker nodes must every Kubernetes cluster have?
notes.back: At least one.
notes.explanation: The worker nodes host the Pods that make up the application.

notes.front: In production, how are the control plane and nodes usually arranged?
notes.back: The control plane runs across multiple computers, and the cluster runs multiple nodes.
notes.explanation: This provides fault tolerance and high availability.

notes.front: Where do simple setup scripts usually start the control plane components?
notes.back: All on the same machine, which does not run user containers.
notes.explanation: Control plane components can run on any machine; spreading them across machines is how highly available clusters are built.

notes.front: Which three components run on every node?
notes.back: The kubelet, kube-proxy (optional) and a container runtime.
notes.explanation: Node components maintain running Pods and provide the Kubernetes runtime environment.

notes.front: In this diagram of a cluster, which component do all the others, including every node, connect to?
notes.back: kube-apiserver (the API server).
notes.explanation: The API server is the front end of the control plane: components communicate through it, not directly with each other.

notes.back: The kubelet and kube-proxy.
notes.explanation: The diagram does not show it, but each node also runs a container runtime.

notes.front: Which word is the legacy synonym for the nodes hosting the control plane?
notes.back: Master.
notes.explanation: Older material says “master node”; current documentation says control plane.

notes.front: What were Nodes called in early Kubernetes versions?
notes.back: Minions.
notes.explanation: Current documentation uses Node.

notes.front: How is kube-apiserver designed to scale?
notes.back: Horizontally: you run more instances and balance traffic between them.
notes.explanation: Several instances can share the load of API requests.

notes.front: Why does an etcd-backed cluster need a backup plan for etcd?
notes.back: Because etcd holds all the cluster’s data.
notes.explanation: Losing etcd means losing the record of every object in the cluster.

notes.front: Which factors does kube-scheduler weigh when choosing a node?
notes.back: Resource needs; hardware, software and policy constraints; affinity and anti-affinity; data locality; interference between workloads; deadlines.
notes.explanation: These are the six factors the glossary lists for its scheduling decisions.

notes.front: How do most Kubernetes controllers bring about the changes they want?
notes.back: By sending messages to the API server, which has other components act on them.
notes.explanation: The controller itself often does not run anything; it asks for the right objects to be created or removed.

notes.front: Some controllers must change things outside the cluster. How do they work?
notes.back: They read the desired state from the API server, act directly on the external system, then report the current state back.
notes.explanation: A controller that adds nodes to a cluster when needed is an example.

notes.front: When does a cluster have no cloud-controller-manager?
notes.back: When it runs on your own premises, or in a learning environment on your own PC.
notes.explanation: The cloud-controller-manager only runs controllers specific to a cloud provider.

notes.front: Which three controllers can depend on a cloud provider?
notes.back: The node controller, the route controller and the service controller.
notes.explanation: They check for deleted cloud nodes, set up cloud routes, and manage cloud load balancers.

notes.front: When can a node do without kube-proxy?
notes.back: When the cluster’s networking add-on (network plugin) forwards Service traffic itself, with behaviour equivalent to kube-proxy.
notes.explanation: That is why the documentation marks kube-proxy as optional.

notes.front: Does the kubelet manage containers that Kubernetes did not create?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The kubelet ensures that the containers described to it are running and healthy, and nothing more.

notes.front: Which addon should every Kubernetes cluster have, because many examples rely on it?
notes.back: Cluster DNS.
notes.explanation: It serves DNS records for Kubernetes Services, and containers include it in their DNS searches automatically.

notes.front: Which addon gives a general-purpose web interface for managing and troubleshooting a cluster?
notes.back: The Web UI, called Dashboard.
notes.explanation: It covers both the applications running in the cluster and the cluster itself.

notes.front: Which addon records time-series metrics about containers in a central database?
notes.back: Container resource monitoring.
notes.explanation: It also provides a user interface for browsing that data.

notes.front: Which addon saves container logs to a central log store with a search interface?
notes.back: Cluster-level logging.
notes.explanation: It provides a search and browsing interface over that central store.

notes.front: In which namespace do the namespaced resources of addons belong?
notes.back: kube-system.
notes.explanation: Addons provide cluster-level features, so they live with the system’s own objects.

notes.front: What is at the core of the Kubernetes control plane?
notes.back: The API server and the HTTP API it exposes.
notes.explanation: Users, parts of the cluster and external components all communicate through it.

notes.front: At which paths are the core API and the named API groups served?
notes.back: The core API at /api/v1; named groups at /apis/<group>/<version>.
notes.explanation: For example, /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1alpha1.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “The Kubernetes API”, “API groups and versioning”

notes.front: Can a generally available (GA) Kubernetes API version be removed?
notes.back: It may be deprecated, but not removed within a major version of Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: GA versions are typically v1; there are no current plans for a major version that removes GA APIs.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Deprecation Policy”, “Deprecating parts of the API”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Can an alpha Kubernetes API version be removed without warning?
notes.back: Yes. Alpha API versions may be removed in any release without prior deprecation notice.
notes.explanation: Check the release notes before upgrading a cluster that uses alpha APIs.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Deprecation Policy”, “Deprecating parts of the API”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Can a beta Kubernetes API version be relied on indefinitely?
notes.back: No. Beta versions have limited lifetimes: they are deprecated and later stop being served, within set time limits.
notes.explanation: Move to the next beta or stable version while the old beta is in its deprecation period.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Deprecation Policy”, “Deprecating parts of the API”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Why is a Kubernetes object called a “record of intent”?
notes.back: Creating it tells Kubernetes what you want; the system then works constantly to make sure it exists.
notes.explanation: The objects together are your cluster’s desired state.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Understanding Kubernetes objects”

notes.front: Who sets an object’s status: you or Kubernetes?
notes.back: Kubernetes and its components; you set the spec.
notes.explanation: The control plane continually manages every object’s actual state to match the desired state you supplied.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Object spec and status”

notes.front: In a manifest, which required field says which version of the Kubernetes API you are using?
notes.back: apiVersion.
notes.explanation: The other required fields are kind, metadata and spec.

notes.front: In a manifest, which required field says what kind of object you want to create?
notes.back: kind.
notes.explanation: The other required fields are apiVersion, metadata and spec.

notes.front: In a manifest, which required field holds data that uniquely identifies the object, such as its name?
notes.back: metadata.
notes.explanation: Metadata includes a name string, a UID and an optional namespace.

notes.front: In a manifest, which required field states what you want the object to be like?
notes.back: spec.
notes.explanation: Its exact format differs for every kind of object.

notes.front: By convention, which format are Kubernetes manifests written in?
notes.back: YAML (JSON also works).
notes.explanation: Tools convert the manifest into JSON or another format when making the API request.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Describing a Kubernetes object”

notes.front: Within one namespace, can a Pod and a Service share the same name?
notes.back: Yes. Names must be unique only among objects of the same kind.
notes.explanation: Two Pods with the same name in the same namespace are not allowed.

notes.front: What is the maximum length of a name that must be a DNS subdomain name?
notes.back: 253 characters.
notes.explanation: It may contain only lowercase letters, digits, “-” and “.”, and must start and end with a letter or digit.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Object Names and IDs”, “DNS Subdomain Names”

notes.front: Across what scope is an object’s UID unique?
notes.back: The whole cluster, over its entire lifetime.
notes.explanation: A name can be reused after deletion; a UID never is.

notes.front: Can namespaces be nested, and can a resource belong to more than one?
notes.back: No to both: namespaces cannot be nested, and each resource is in exactly one namespace.
notes.explanation: Namespaces provide a scope for names.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Namespaces”, “When to Use Multiple Namespaces”

notes.front: Are Nodes namespaced objects?
notes.back: No. Nodes are cluster-wide objects; namespaces apply only to namespaced objects.
notes.explanation: Namespaced examples include Services; cluster-wide ones include Nodes and StorageClasses.

notes.front: When does the Kubernetes documentation suggest starting to use multiple namespaces?
notes.back: When many users are spread across multiple teams or projects.
notes.explanation: For a few to tens of users you should not need to think about namespaces; use labels to tell versions apart.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Namespaces”, “When to Use Multiple Namespaces”

notes.front: How many namespaces does a new Kubernetes cluster start with?
notes.back: Four.
notes.explanation: They are default, kube-node-lease, kube-public and kube-system.

notes.front: Which initial namespace exists so you can use a new cluster without creating a namespace first?
notes.back: default.
notes.explanation: For a production cluster, the documentation advises creating other namespaces instead of using default.

notes.front: Which initial namespace holds the small objects each node’s kubelet updates regularly to say “I’m alive” (heartbeats)?
notes.back: kube-node-lease.
notes.explanation: The heartbeats let the control plane detect when a node fails.

notes.front: Which initial namespace is readable by all clients, including unauthenticated ones?
notes.back: kube-public.
notes.explanation: It is mostly reserved for cluster use; being public is a convention, not a requirement.

notes.front: Which initial namespace holds objects created by the Kubernetes system?
notes.back: kube-system.
notes.explanation: Avoid creating your own namespaces with the kube- prefix, which is reserved for system namespaces.

notes.front: Do labels identify a single object uniquely?
notes.back: No. Many objects are expected to carry the same labels; names and UIDs provide uniqueness.
notes.explanation: Labels exist to group objects, which is why selectors work on them.

notes.front: Which two types of label selector does the Kubernetes API support?
notes.back: Equality-based and set-based.
notes.explanation: Equality-based uses =, == and !=; set-based uses in, notin and exists.

notes.front: In a label selector with several comma-separated requirements, how are they combined?
notes.back: With logical AND: all must be satisfied. There is no “or” operator.
notes.explanation: Structure your filters with this in mind.

notes.front: How long may a label value, or the name part of a label key, be?
notes.back: 63 characters or less.
notes.explanation: An optional prefix on the key, a DNS subdomain, may be up to 253 characters.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Labels and Selectors”, “Syntax and character set”

notes.front: Which label key prefixes are reserved for Kubernetes core components?
notes.back: kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/.
notes.explanation: Automated components that add labels to users’ objects must use a prefix.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Labels and Selectors”, “Syntax and character set”

notes.front: Can annotations hold data that labels cannot?
notes.back: Yes. Annotations can be large or small, structured or unstructured, and include characters labels do not allow.
notes.explanation: Both are key/value maps in an object’s metadata; only labels are used for selecting.

notes.front: Is ownership between objects the same mechanism as labels and selectors?
notes.back: No. Owner references are a separate field that tells Kubernetes which objects depend on which.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes sets owner references automatically in most cases.

notes.front: What happens when you delete an object that has finalizers?
notes.back: It is marked for deletion and stays until controllers finish their clean-up and remove every finalizer; then it is deleted.
notes.explanation: The API marks it by setting metadata.deletionTimestamp and replies with HTTP 202 (Accepted).

notes.front: How long are Kubernetes Events kept, and how far can you rely on them?
notes.back: For a limited time only; treat them as informative, best-effort, supplemental data.
notes.explanation: Their triggers and messages may also change over time.

notes.front: What are the two ways to extend the Kubernetes API with custom resources?
notes.back: CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) and the aggregation layer (API aggregation).
notes.explanation: CRDs need no programming; aggregation needs programming but gives more control.

notes.front: What does a CRD spare you from writing?
notes.back: Your own API server: the Kubernetes API serves and stores the custom resource for you.
notes.explanation: The trade-off is less flexibility than API server aggregation.

notes.front: What turns a custom resource from mere data storage into a true declarative API?
notes.back: Combining it with a custom controller.
notes.explanation: On its own, a custom resource only lets you store and retrieve structured data.

notes.front: In relation to the Kubernetes API, what is an operator?
notes.back: A client of the API that acts as a controller for a custom resource.
notes.explanation: Operators follow Kubernetes principles, notably the control loop.

notes.front: How do you turn a feature gate on or off for a Kubernetes component?
notes.back: With that component’s --feature-gates command-line flag.
notes.explanation: Each component has its own relevant set of feature gates.

notes.front: A system restarts crashed containers, scales them with demand and corrects any drift from the declared state. What is it doing?
notes.back: Container orchestration.
notes.explanation: Orchestrators automate the lifecycle of containerised applications.

notes.front: A team expects Kubernetes to come with a built-in database and a fixed monitoring stack, like a traditional PaaS. What should they be told?
notes.back: Kubernetes provides neither: it is not an all-inclusive PaaS, and such components are optional and pluggable.
notes.explanation: Databases can run on Kubernetes, and you choose your own monitoring.

notes.front: Does kube-apiserver run in the control plane or on every worker node?
notes.back: In the control plane.
notes.explanation: Control plane components manage the overall state of the cluster.

notes.front: Is etcd a control plane component or a node component?
notes.back: A control plane component.
notes.explanation: It stores all the API server’s data.

notes.front: Is kube-scheduler a control plane component or a node component?
notes.back: A control plane component.
notes.explanation: Scheduling is a global decision about the cluster.

notes.front: Is kube-controller-manager a control plane component or a node component?
notes.back: A control plane component.
notes.explanation: It runs the controllers that implement Kubernetes API behaviour.

notes.front: Is cloud-controller-manager a control plane component or a node component, and is it required?
notes.back: An optional control plane component.
notes.explanation: It integrates the cluster with the underlying cloud provider.

notes.front: Does the kubelet run in the control plane or on every node?
notes.back: On every node.
notes.explanation: It ensures that Pods, including their containers, are running.

notes.front: Does kube-proxy run in the control plane or on the nodes, and is it required?
notes.back: On every node, and it is optional.
notes.explanation: It maintains network rules on nodes to implement Services.

notes.front: Is the container runtime a control plane component or a node component?
notes.back: A node component.
notes.explanation: It is the software responsible for running containers on each node.

notes.front: A newly created Pod has no node assigned yet. Which component will choose one for it?
notes.back: kube-scheduler.
notes.explanation: The kubelet on the chosen node then makes sure the Pod’s containers run.

notes.front: An administrator wants to back up all of a cluster’s state. Which component’s data must be backed up?
notes.back: etcd’s.
notes.explanation: etcd is the backing store for all cluster data.

notes.front: On one node, a container has stopped and must be restarted. Which component on that node makes sure it runs again?
notes.back: The kubelet.
notes.explanation: The kubelet ensures the containers it is given are running and healthy.

notes.front: The number of running copies of an application has fallen below what its object asks for. Which control plane component runs the loop that notices and corrects this?
notes.back: kube-controller-manager, through one of its controllers.
notes.explanation: Controllers compare current with desired state and act to close the gap.

notes.front: A cluster running on a public cloud must create the provider’s load balancers and routes. Which component handles this?
notes.back: The cloud-controller-manager.
notes.explanation: Its service and route controllers talk to the cloud provider’s API.

notes.front: Traffic sent to a Service must reach one of its Pods on whichever node they run. Which node component maintains the rules for this?
notes.back: kube-proxy (unless a network plugin replaces it).
notes.explanation: Its network rules allow sessions from inside or outside the cluster to reach Pods.

notes.front: A command-line tool wants to create an object in the cluster. Which component does its request go to?
notes.back: kube-apiserver.
notes.explanation: Most operations use tools that call the API server’s HTTP API.

notes.front: A thermostat keeps a room at 20 °C by switching the heating on and off. Which Kubernetes concept works the same way?
notes.back: A controller (a control loop).
notes.explanation: It watches the current state and acts to bring it closer to the desired state.

notes.front: An object asks for three copies of an app, but two are running. Which field holds “three”, and which “two”?
notes.back: “Three” is in the spec (desired state); “two” is in the status (current state).
notes.explanation: Kubernetes responds to the difference by starting a replacement.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Object spec and status”

notes.front: A YAML file sets apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec for an object you want. What is the file called?
notes.back: A manifest.
notes.explanation: A manifest specifies the desired state of an object in JSON or YAML.

notes.front: A Kubernetes entity is persistent, represents part of the cluster’s state and is a record of your intent. What is it?
notes.back: An object.
notes.explanation: Objects together describe the cluster’s desired state.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Understanding Kubernetes objects”

notes.front: The path /apis/rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1alpha1 contains rbac.authorization.k8s.io. What is that part?
notes.back: The API group.
notes.explanation: Named groups are served at /apis/<group>/<version>; the core group is at /api/v1.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “The Kubernetes API”, “API groups and versioning”

notes.front: An object was created through v1beta1 of its API, and v1 is now available. Can you read it through v1?
notes.back: Yes. Versions are different representations of the same stored data.
notes.explanation: Do so before v1beta1 is deprecated and removed.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “The Kubernetes API”, “API groups and versioning”

notes.front: A production cluster relies on an alpha API version. What is the risk at the next upgrade?
notes.back: The API may change incompatibly or be removed without prior notice.
notes.explanation: Alpha API versions may be removed in any release; read the release notes first.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Deprecation Policy”, “Deprecating parts of the API”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Two teams share one cluster and both want a Service called web. How can they avoid a clash?
notes.back: Put each team’s objects in its own namespace; names must be unique only within a namespace.
notes.explanation: Namespaces isolate groups of resources within a single cluster.

notes.front: You want to mark Pods with the environment they belong to, such as production or qa, so you can pick them out later. What should you use?
notes.back: Labels, such as environment: production.
notes.explanation: Labels are identifying attributes that can be selected on.

notes.front: You need to act on every object labelled tier: frontend. What do you use to identify them?
notes.back: A label selector.
notes.explanation: An equality-based requirement such as tier = frontend matches them.

notes.front: You want to record the build number and a contact address on an object, without using them to select it. What should you use?
notes.back: Annotations.
notes.explanation: Annotations hold non-identifying metadata; labels are for identifying and selecting.

notes.front: You see a short-lived record saying the scheduler assigned a Pod to a node. What kind of object is it?
notes.back: An Event.
notes.explanation: Events describe state changes or notable occurrences in the cluster.

notes.front: You want users to create objects of a new type, “Backup”, without writing your own API server. What do you create?
notes.back: A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD).
notes.explanation: Defining a CRD creates a new custom resource that the Kubernetes API serves and stores.

notes.front: You want software that runs in the cluster and automatically installs, backs up and upgrades a complex database, as an expert would. Which pattern is this?
notes.back: The operator pattern.
notes.explanation: An operator links a controller to custom resources describing the database.

notes.front: A web interface, installed on top of the core components, lets you manage and troubleshoot applications in the cluster. What category of Kubernetes component is it?
notes.back: An addon (the Dashboard).
notes.explanation: Addons extend the functionality of Kubernetes.

notes.front: A company runs its containerised apps on three worker machines, managed by a Kubernetes control plane. What do the machines and control plane form together?
notes.back: A Kubernetes cluster.
notes.explanation: A cluster is a control plane plus a set of worker nodes that run containerised applications.

notes.front: You delete a Pod called cache-1 and then create a new Pod called cache-1. Is the name allowed?
notes.back: Yes. A name only has to be unique among existing objects of that kind, so it can be reused after deletion.
notes.explanation: Only one object of a given kind can have a given name at a time.

notes.front: The old and new Pods called cache-1 must be told apart in the cluster’s history. Which identifier does that?
notes.back: The UID.
notes.explanation: Every object created over the lifetime of a cluster gets a distinct, system-generated UID.

notes.front: Where would you expect to find the objects that the Kubernetes system itself creates?
notes.back: In the kube-system namespace.
notes.explanation: It is one of the four initial namespaces, alongside default, kube-node-lease and kube-public.

notes.front: Objects of type SampleDB exist in a cluster only because an extension added that type to its API. What are they?
notes.back: Custom resources.
notes.explanation: They extend the Kubernetes API beyond the built-in resources, such as Pods.

notes.front: What is the difference between the control plane and the worker nodes?
notes.back: The control plane manages the cluster and makes global decisions; the worker nodes host the Pods that run the application.
notes.explanation: In small clusters they can share machines; production clusters usually separate them.

notes.front: What is the difference between kube-controller-manager and cloud-controller-manager?
notes.back: kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers; cloud-controller-manager runs only those that depend on a cloud provider.
notes.explanation: A cluster on your own premises has no cloud-controller-manager.

notes.front: What is the difference between an object’s spec and its status?
notes.back: The spec is the desired state you set; the status is the current state, set by Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: The control plane works to make the status match the spec.
notes.contrast: What you want, versus what is.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Objects In Kubernetes”, “Object spec and status”

notes.front: What is the difference between an object’s name and its UID?
notes.back: You choose the name, which is unique per kind and can be reused later; the system generates the UID, unique for the cluster’s lifetime.
notes.explanation: Labels and annotations cover attributes that are not unique.
notes.contrast: Chosen and reusable, versus generated and never reused.

notes.front: What is the difference between a label and an annotation?
notes.back: Labels identify objects and can be selected on; annotations hold non-identifying metadata and are not used for selection.
notes.explanation: Both are key/value pairs in the object’s metadata.
notes.contrast: For finding objects, versus for describing them.

notes.front: What is the difference between adding custom resources with a CRD and with API aggregation?
notes.back: CRDs need no programming; aggregation means writing your own API server, which gives more control over behaviour and storage.
notes.explanation: Either way, the new resources are called custom resources.
notes.contrast: Simple and generic, versus programmed and flexible.

notes.front: How do alpha, beta and GA Kubernetes API versions differ in lifetime?
notes.back: Alpha may vanish in any release; beta is deprecated and retired within set limits; GA is not removed within a major version.
notes.explanation: The more stable the level, the stronger the compatibility promise.
notes.contrast: No promise, versus a limited promise, versus a lasting one.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Deprecation Policy”, “Deprecating parts of the API”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date
